name: Jeremiah
v: Zedekiah was twenty-one when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes — every bit as bad as Jehoiakim before him.
It was the LORD's fury that drove what happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until finally he hurled them out of his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

So in the ninth year of his reign, the tenth month, the tenth day — Nebuchadnezzar came. The whole Babylonian army came with him. They camped against Jerusalem and threw up siege walls around it on every side.
The city stayed under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine inside had become brutal. There was no bread left for anyone.

Then the wall was breached. Every soldier ran. They slipped out of the city by night through the gate between the two walls, by the king's garden — the Babylonians had the city surrounded — and they fled toward the Arabah.
But the Babylonian army chased the king and caught up with Zedekiah on the plains of Jericho. His whole army scattered, leaving him alone.
They seized him and hauled him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, where sentence was pronounced.
There the king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah's sons in front of him. He slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah.
Then he gouged out Zedekiah's eyes, shackled him in bronze chains, and took him to Babylon. He locked him in prison until the day he died.
In the fifth month, on the tenth day — the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar — Nebuzaradan, captain of the imperial guard, entered Jerusalem on behalf of the king of Babylon.
He burned the house of the LORD. He burned the royal palace. He burned every house in Jerusalem — every important building went up in flames.
The Babylonian army under his command tore down every wall surrounding Jerusalem.

Nebuzaradan rounded up the poor who remained, the survivors still inside the city, the defectors who had crossed over to the king of Babylon, and what was left of the skilled craftsmen — and he marched them into exile.
But Nebuzaradan left some of the poorest in the land behind to tend the vineyards and work the fields.
The Babylonians shattered the bronze pillars of the LORD's house, the bronze stands, the bronze Sea — and they carried all the bronze back to Babylon.
They took the pots, the shovels, the wick trimmers, the basins, the dishes — every bronze vessel used in the temple service.
The captain of the guard also took the bowls, the firepans, the basins, the pots, the lampstands, the dishes, and the libation cups — anything of pure gold, anything of pure silver, he took.
The two pillars, the one Sea, the twelve bronze bulls beneath it, the stands — what Solomon had made for the house of the LORD — the bronze of all of it was beyond weighing.
Each pillar stood eighteen cubits high, twelve cubits around, hollow, the metal four fingers thick.
On top sat a bronze capital, five cubits tall, ringed with network and pomegranates, all bronze. The second pillar matched, pomegranates and all.
Ninety-six pomegranates faced outward. The total on the network: a hundred, all the way around.
The captain of the guard seized Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three doorkeepers.

From the city he took an officer who had commanded the soldiers, seven of the king's personal advisors found in the city, the scribe of the army commander who conscripted the people, and sixty men of the land caught inside the city.
Nebuzaradan took them all and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
There, at Riblah in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon executed them. So Judah went into exile, far from its own soil.
These are the numbers Nebuchadnezzar deported: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans.
In his eighteenth year, 832 souls from Jerusalem.
In his twenty-third year, Nebuzaradan deported 745 more Judeans. Total: 4,600.

In the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile — the twelfth month, the twenty-fifth day — Evil-merodach became king of Babylon, and in his first year he lifted Jehoiachin's head and brought him out of prison.
He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes. He ate at the king's table for the rest of his life.
And his allowance — a steady, daily allowance from the king of Babylon — kept coming, every day, until the day he died.

com.d:
# Jeremiah 52: The Lord's Faithfulness Beyond Judgment

In Jeremiah's final chapter, we witness both the terrible culmination of Jerusalem's destruction and the fragile spark of hope that emerges from exile. This passage testifies that God's faithfulness persists even when his judgment comes to pass, and that redemption can break through the darkest circumstances.

The fall of Jerusalem is presented with unflinching honesty. King Zedekiah's reign crumbles under Babylonian siege; the temple burns; and the people are led away captive. Every word confirms Jeremiah's decades of weeping prophecy. There is profound pastoral wisdom here: sometimes faith means watching what God warned actually happen, and choosing to believe anyway. The people had rejected the prophet's message, yet his words proved true, which paradoxically becomes evidence of God's truthfulness and the reliability of his word.

Yet the chapter does not end in ash. Instead, it closes with Jehoiachin, the deposed king, being shown mercy in exile. After thirty-seven years in prison, he receives a pardon, is released, and given food and favor in the Babylonian court. This is not restoration to the throne—the wound is real and ongoing—but it is restoration of dignity. A remnant survives. A seed remains for God to work with.

This ending illuminates a profound truth: God does not abandon his people in captivity. Judgment is real, and consequences persist, but they are not the final word. Those who face the hard consequences of their waywardness discover that God meets them there with measured mercy. This speaks powerfully to anyone trudging through the aftermath of failure, facing seasons of loss, or living with the real weight of poor choices. The path forward may be difficult and long, but it is not utterly severed from hope.

What circumstance in your life feels like you're living in exile? Can you glimpse, even faintly, how God might be preserving something precious in the midst of it?
com.s:
Jeremiah 52 functions as a historical appendix to the prophetic book, largely paralleling the account found in 2 Kings 24:18–25:30, though with notable variations that suggest editorial intentionality in its placement. This chapter was almost certainly not composed by Jeremiah himself, as indicated by the concluding notice in Jeremiah 51:64 ("Thus far the words of Jeremiah"), yet its inclusion serves the crucial theological purpose of vindicating the prophet's warnings against Jerusalem and demonstrating the fulfillment of divine judgment proclaimed throughout the preceding oracles.

The narrative recounts Zedekiah's eleven-year reign and subsequent rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, culminating in the catastrophic siege and fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE. The Hebrew term *matsōr* (siege) appears prominently, evoking the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:52–57 and establishing this destruction as the inevitable consequence of persistent covenant violation. Particularly striking is the detailed account of Zedekiah's capture at the plains of Jericho (*ʿarḇōṯ yerīḥō*), where the blinded king witnesses his sons' execution—a brutal reversal that underscores the totality of Davidic humiliation.

The chapter's extensive inventory of temple vessels—the bronze pillars, the sea, and various cultic implements—serves more than antiquarian interest. The Hebrew *nĕḥōšeṯ* (bronze) recurs emphatically throughout verses 17–23, cataloging the systematic dismantling of Solomon's architectural achievement. This detailed accounting transforms destruction into theological testimony, demonstrating that Yahweh's glory had indeed departed from the sanctuary as Ezekiel's contemporary visions proclaimed.

The deportation figures in verses 28–30, which differ from those in 2 Kings, have generated considerable scholarly discussion regarding their relationship to other biblical and extrabiblical sources. Some interpreters suggest these represent distinct deportation waves or perhaps enumerate only adult males. The chapter's conclusion with Jehoiachin's elevation in Babylon (verses 31–34) introduces an unexpected note of hope within devastation. The verb *nāśāʾ* (to lift up) applied to Jehoiachin's head suggests the preservation of Davidic lineage amid exile, gesturing toward future restoration. This ending transforms the entire chapter from mere chronicle into theological witness, affirming that judgment, though severe, remains bounded by divine faithfulness to covenantal promises.
com.p:
Jeremiah chapter fifty-two stands as the somber historical epilogue to the prophetic ministry of the weeping prophet, recording events that transpired in 586 BC when Nebuchadnezzar's Babylonian forces finally breached Jerusalem's walls after an eighteen-month siege. This chapter, nearly identical to 2 Kings 25, was appended to Jeremiah's prophecies as vindication—every word the prophet spoke against the unrepentant kingdom of Judah came to devastating fulfillment within his lifetime.

On the great timeline of redemption, this chapter marks the nadir of the Davidic kingdom, the catastrophic end of the monarchy that began with such promise under David and Solomon. The exile to Babylon represents God's covenant lawsuit against His unfaithful people reaching its terrible verdict. Yet this is not the end of the story—it falls within the Exile phase that would give way to Restoration, pointing forward to a greater King and an unshakeable kingdom.

The details recorded here carry profound typological weight. Zedekiah, the last Davidic king, watched his sons slaughtered before Babylonian soldiers gouged out his eyes—the final image seared into his memory being the death of the royal line. This anti-coronation, this stripping of kingship, shadows by darkest contrast the true King who would come through David's line, whose eyes would close in death only to open in resurrection glory. The temple vessels carried to Babylon, meticulously catalogued in verses seventeen through twenty-three, represent the departure of sacred worship from Jerusalem, yet these same vessels would return under Cyrus—a pattern of death and resurrection woven into Israel's very institutions.

The burning of Solomon's temple, the destruction of the bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz that proclaimed God's establishment and strength, seemed to announce Yahweh's final abandonment. Yet the prophecy required this demolition so that Ezekiel's temple vision and ultimately the incarnate Temple—Christ Himself—could emerge. What human hands built, human hands destroyed; what God builds in Christ can never be torn down.

The chapter closes with an unexpected note of hope: Jehoiachin's release from Babylonian prison and his seat at the king's table. This small mercy preserved the Davidic line through whom Messiah would come. For the church dwelling between advents, Jeremiah fifty-two declares that God's judgments are certain, His Word utterly reliable, and even in the ashes of human failure, He preserves a remnant and a royal seed through whom all nations find blessing.
